Description: explicit — GeoJSON vs tiles decision for a real scenario
prompt: I have about 8,000 hiking trail segments stored as GeoJSON, and users need to click a trail to see its name and distance. I also need a basemap showing terrain and roads. How should I set up the data sources in MapLibre — do I need vector tiles, or can I use GeoJSON?

Description: implicit — dataset outgrew GeoJSON without the user naming tiles
prompt: My parcel layer is a 180 MB GeoJSON file with around 400,000 polygons. The browser hangs for ages on load and sometimes the tab just dies. I've already tried minifying the JSON. What now?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**TL;DR** – A 180 MB / 400 k-polygon GeoJSON is far beyond what a browser can parse and keep alive. The only reliable fix is to **stop sending the whole file to the client** and serve the data as **tiles** (vector tiles if you need interactivity, raster tiles if you only need a picture). Below is a step-by-step decision tree, the concrete tools you can use, and the exact MapLibre code you’ll need once the tiles are ready. --- ## 1️⃣ Why the current approach will never work | Metric | What you have | What the browser can handle | |--------|---------------|-----------------------------| | **File size** | 180 MB (raw JSON) | Even gzipped it’s ~30–40 MB – still huge to download & parse in one go | | **Feature count** | ~400 k polygons | Parsing > 100 k features usually freezes the main thread; memory spikes → tab crash | | **Geometry complexity** | Many vertices per polygon (often > 100 pts) | Each vertex is a JS number → ~8 bytes → 400 k × 100 pts ≈ 320 MB of raw JS objects before any rendering | Minifying the JSON only removes whitespace; it does **not** reduce the number of vertices, the coordinate precision, or the amount of work the browser must do to turn the text into objects. --- ## 2️⃣ Choose the right source type | Situation | Recommended MapLibre source type | Why | |-----------|----------------------------------|-----| | **< 5 k simple features** | `geojson` (inline or URL) | Small enough to download & parse instantly | | **5 k – 100 k features** (still < ~20 MB) | `geojson` **only if** you can heavily simplify & reduce precision | Acceptable latency, but you’ll be close to the “lag zone” | | **> 100 k features** **or** > 20 MB | **Vector tiles** (`type: "vector"`). Use `tippecanoe`, `Planetiler`, or similar to generate them. | Loads only the tiles that intersect the viewport, keeps file size per tile < 50 KB, gives you interactivity & styling flexibility | | **You only need a picture of the parcels** (no click/hover) | **Raster tiles** (`type: "raster"`). Render the polygons on the server once and serve PNG/JPEG tiles. | No client-side geometry, smallest bandwidth, simplest server | > **Bottom line:** For a 400 k-polygon dataset you **must** go to vector tiles (or raster tiles if you can sacrifice interactivity). --- ## 3️⃣ Preparing the data for tiling ### 3.1 Simplify & clean the geometry 1. **Remove unnecessary vertices** – most polygon outlines can be simplified dramatically without visual impact. ```bash # Using mapshaper (fast, CLI) mapshaper parcels.geojson \ -simplify dp 10% keep-shapes \ -filter-islands \ -o format=geojson parcels_simplified.geojson ``` *`dp 10%`* keeps 10 % of the original points (adjust until the visual quality is acceptable). 2. **Reduce coordinate precision** – 5–6 decimal places (~10 cm at the equator) is usually enough. ```bash mapshaper parcels_simplified.geojson \ -precision 6 \ -o format=geojson parcels_precise.geojson ``` 3. **Optional: Convert to TopoJSON** – shares line strings between adjacent polygons, cutting size by ~30 % for dense polygon layers. ```bash topojson -o parcels.topojson -p properties=yourProps parcels_precise.geojson ``` *TopoJSON is still a single file, so you’ll still need tiling, but it reduces the size you feed into the tile generator.* ### 3.2 Generate vector tiles #### Option A – **tippecanoe** (quick, works on any GeoJSON) ```bash # Install tippecanoe (brew, apt, or from source) # Create an MBTiles file (or PMTiles) with a sensible zoom range. tippecanoe \ --output parcels.mbtiles \ --layer parcels \ --minimum-zoom=5 \ --maximum-zoom=14 \ --drop-densest-as-needed \ --simplify-only-low-zoom \ --no-feature-limit \ --no-tile-size-limit \ parcels_precise.geojson ``` *Key flags* | Flag | What it does | |------|---------------| | `--minimum-zoom` / `--maximum-zoom` | Limits the zoom levels you actually need (no point generating z = 0-2 for a parcel layer). | | `--drop-densest-as-needed` | If a tile would exceed the default 500 KB limit, tippecanoe drops the densest features automatically. | | `--simplify-only-low-zoom` | Keeps full detail at high zooms, but aggressively simplifies at low zooms (where you don’t need every parcel edge). | | `--no-feature-limit` / `--no-tile-size-limit` | Turn off hard caps if you want to control them yourself (use with caution). | **Result:** `parcels.mbtiles` (SQLite) or, with `--output-format=pmtiles`, a single `parcels.pmtiles` file that can be served statically. #### Option B – **Planetiler** (if you already have OSM-style pipelines or need custom attribute handling) ```bash # Build a simple Java project or use the Docker image docker run -v $(pwd):/data onthegomap/planetiler \ --input /data/parcels_precise.geojson \ --output /data/parcels.pmtiles \ --layer parcels \ --minzoom 5 --maxzoom 14 ``` Planetiler gives you more control over attribute indexing and can produce **MapLibre Tile (MLT)** format directly. ### 3.3 Host the tiles | Hosting method | When to use | |----------------|-------------| | **Static file server (NGINX, GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Workers)** | Small MBTiles/PMTiles files (< 500 MB) that you can serve whole-file with range requests. | | **PMTiles serverless pattern** (`maplibre-pmtiles-patterns` skill) | You want a single-file archive that works with CORS and works on any static host. | | **Tile server (TileServer GL, Tileserver-PHP, t-rex, or TileStache)** | You need dynamic tile generation, multiple layers, or per-tile caching. | | **Commercial tile service (MapTiler Cloud, OpenFreeMap, etc.)** | You don’t want to manage any infrastructure. | > **Tip:** If you go the PMTiles route, you can serve the file directly from a CDN (S3 + CloudFront, Azure Blob, etc.) – the browser will request only the byte ranges it needs. --- ## 4️⃣ Wire the tiles into MapLibre ### 4.1 Vector-tile source (PMTiles) ```javascript // Assuming you have parcels.pmtiles hosted at https://cdn.example.com/parcels.pmtiles map.addSource('parcels', { type: 'vector', url: 'pmtiles://https://cdn.example.com/parcels.pmtiles' // pmtiles:// protocol handled by maplibre-pmtiles plugin }); ``` If you are using a classic MBTiles endpoint (served via TileServer-GL or similar): ```javascript map.addSource('parcels', { type: 'vector', url: 'https://tiles.example.com/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf' // TileJSON can also be used }); ``` ### 4.2 Add a layer ```javascript map.addLayer({ id: 'parcels-fill', type: 'fill', source: 'parcels', 'source-layer': 'parcels', // name you gave with tippecanoe (--layer parcels) paint: { 'fill-color': '#ff6600', 'fill-opacity': 0.4, 'fill-outline-color': '#ff3300' } }); ``` If you need a line outline on top: ```javascript map.addLayer({ id: 'parcels-outline', type: 'line', source: 'parcels', 'source-layer': 'parcels', paint: { 'line-color': '#ff3300', 'line-width': 1 } }); ``` ### 4.3 Interactivity (click/hover) ```javascript map.on('click', 'parcels-fill', (e) => { const props = e.features[0].properties; new maplibregl.Popup() .setLngLat(e.lngLat) .setHTML(`Parcel ID: ${props.id}
Owner: ${props.owner}`) .addTo(map); }); ``` Because the data are now **tiles**, the browser only parses the few kilobytes that intersect the current view, and `queryRenderedFeatures` works instantly. --- ## 5️⃣ If you *cannot* generate tiles (quick-and-dirty fallback) | Approach | Pros | Cons | |----------|------|------| | **client-side tiling with `geojson-vt`** | No server work; you keep a single GeoJSON file | Still needs to download the whole 180 MB → same crash problem; only useful for *much* smaller files | | **Chunked loading (multiple GeoJSON files, one per tile grid)** | You can keep the GeoJSON format | You must write a custom loader that swaps files in/out; you lose the compactness of true vector tiles | | **Render to raster on the server (e.g., MapServer, GeoServer) and serve as raster tiles** | No client geometry, fast rendering | No feature-level interactivity; you lose the ability to style on the fly | These are *stop-gap* measures; they do not solve the fundamental bandwidth & memory problem. --- ## 6️⃣ Checklist – What to do next 1. **Simplify & reduce precision** of the original GeoJSON (mapshaper → `--simplify dp 10%` + `--precision 6`). 2. **Generate vector tiles** with tippecanoe (or Planetiler) targeting the zoom range you actually need (e.g., 5-14). 3. **Host the resulting MBTiles/PMTiles** on a static CDN or a lightweight tile server. 4. **Add a `vector` source** to your MapLibre style and create the fill/line layers. 5. **Test on a low-end device** (mobile, older laptop) – you should see < 200 ms tile fetch + < 50 ms render at typical zooms. 6. (Optional) If you need **offline** usage, the PMTiles file can be bundled with the app and loaded via the `pmtiles://` protocol without any network request. --- ## 7️⃣ Quick “one-liner” answer you can copy-paste > *Your 180 MB, 400 k-polygon GeoJSON is far beyond the practical limits of the `geojson` source (the “crash zone”). The only robust solution is to turn the data into vector tiles (e.g., with tippecanoe) and serve them as a `vector` source. Simplify the geometry first (mapshaper –-simplify dp 10% –-precision 6), generate an MBTiles/PMTiles archive, host it on a CDN or a tiny tile server, then add it to MapLibre

Description: anti-pattern — merging basemap and application data into one tileset
prompt: I want my roads, water, labels, and my own delivery-zone polygons all in a single vector tileset so the map only hits one source. What's the best pipeline to merge OpenStreetMap data with my polygons and build that combined tileset?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:** For almost every web-map you’ll get a more maintainable, cheaper-to-update and legally-safer solution by **keeping the basemap (roads, water, labels) as one vector-tile source and your delivery-zone polygons as a second source** (GeoJSON or its own vector-tile source). MapLibre can request both sources in parallel with no performance penalty, and you keep the basemap’s styling, attribution and update cycle separate from your data. Below is a two-part response: 1. **Why “one source” isn’t the right optimisation** – the reasoning you should give the user. 2. **If you truly need a single combined tileset** – a concrete, production-ready pipeline (tools, steps, gotchas) that merges OSM data with your polygons. --- ## 1️⃣ Why a single combined tileset is usually a bad idea | Reason | Explanation | |--------|-------------| | **No rendering cost for extra sources** | MapLibre opens *all* sources concurrently. Adding a second source does **not** add a per-source rendering penalty; the only cost is the extra HTTP request(s) for the tiles you already need. | | **Separate update cycles** | OSM basemap data is refreshed weekly (or daily on many providers). Your delivery-zone polygons change on a completely different schedule. If they live in the same tileset you must rebuild the *entire* tileset every time a single polygon changes. | | **Licensing & attribution** | OSM data carries the ODbL/CC-BY-SA attribution. When you bake it into a custom tileset you become a redistributor and must embed that attribution in the tileset metadata and in your UI. Keeping the basemap as a hosted style (e.g. from OpenFreeMap, MapTiler, or a public OSM vector-tile service) lets you rely on the provider’s attribution handling. | | **Styling flexibility** | Vector tiles are styled client-side. If the basemap and your data share a tileset you lose the ability to change the basemap style without rebuilding the tiles. Two sources let you swap the basemap style URL instantly. | | **Complexity & build time** | Merging a planet-scale OSM extract with a few hundred delivery-zone polygons forces you to run a full-planet tile generation pipeline (tippecanoe/Planetiler) just to add a tiny amount of data. That is orders of magnitude slower and more resource-hungry than generating a small overlay tileset. | | **Offline-only exception** | The only common case for a single file is an *offline* kiosk or air-gapped demo where you cannot make any network request at all. Even then you can ship two small PMTiles files side-by-side; the overhead is negligible. | **Bottom line:** > *“One source” is not a performance optimisation. Use two sources: a hosted OSM vector-tile source for the basemap, and a separate source for your delivery-zone polygons.* --- ## 2️⃣ If you really need a single combined vector-tile set – a production-grade pipeline > **Caveat:** Follow this only if you have a compelling offline-only requirement or you are building a completely self-contained demo. Otherwise, use the two-source pattern described above. ### Overview diagram ``` OSM extract (PBF) ──► (filter & re-project) ──► Tile generator (tippecanoe / Planetiler) ──► │ Your polygons (GeoJSON/FlatGeobuf) ──► (merge) ────────────────────────────────────────► ▼ Combined vector-tile archive (PMTiles / MBTiles) ──► HTTP server (or static CDN) ──► MapLibre style → map ``` ### Step-by-step | # | Action | Tool(s) | Key options / notes | |---|--------|---------|----------------------| | **1** | **Obtain an OSM extract** that covers the area you need (country, region, or the whole planet). | • Geofabrik (download `.pbf`),
• BBBike,
• OSM “planet” dump. | Keep the extract as small as possible – the smaller the source, the faster the later tile generation. | | **2** | **Clip the OSM extract** to the exact bounding box of your delivery service (optional but speeds up the build). | `osmium extract -b source.osm.pbf clipped.osm.pbf`
or `osmconvert`. | Use the same CRS (WGS-84) that MapLibre expects (`EPSG:4326`). | | **3** | **Prepare your delivery-zone polygons** in a format that can be merged with OSM data. | • GeoJSON,
• FlatGeobuf,
• Parquet (via `ogr2ogr`). | Ensure the geometry is valid (no self-intersections) and simplified to an appropriate level (e.g., `--simplify 0.5` in `ogr2ogr`). | | **4** | **Convert your polygons to OSM-compatible PBF** (optional but makes merging easier). | `ogr2ogr -f "OSM" myzones.osm.pbf myzones.geojson` | Add a custom OSM tag namespace (e.g., `delivery_zone=yes`) so you can later reference the layer. | | **5** | **Merge the two PBF files** into a single OSM dataset. | `osmium merge clipped.osm.pbf myzones.osm.pbf -o merged.osm.pbf` | Preserve all tags; you can also use `osmium tags-filter` to drop unwanted tags from the OSM side if you want a leaner tileset. | | **6** | **Generate vector tiles** from the merged OSM PBF. Two mainstream options: | | | **Option A – tippecanoe** (good for < 10 M features, fast, simple) | **Option B – Planetiler** (scales to planet-size, more control) | |---|---------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------| | **Command** | `tippecanoe -o combined.pmtiles --layer roads --layer water --layer waterway --layer landuse --layer place --layer admin --layer delivery_zones --drop-densest-as-needed --maximum-zoom=14 --minimum-zoom=5 merged.osm.pbf` | Build a small Java project (or use the pre-built Docker image) that reads the merged PBF, registers a custom layer for your polygons, and writes an MVT/PMTiles archive. | | **Key flags** | • `--layer ` creates separate source-layers (you’ll need one for each OSM feature class you want to style).
• `--drop-densest-as-needed` keeps tile size < 500 KB.
• `--force` to overwrite.
• `--read-parallel` for multi-core. | • Define a `FeatureProcessor` for OSM tags you care about.
• Add a `FeatureProcessor` for your custom `delivery_zone` tag.
• Set `maxZoom`/`minZoom` per layer. | | **Output** | `combined.pmtiles` (or `combined.mbtiles`). | Same – you can output PMTiles for server-less hosting. | | **When to choose** | Small-to-medium projects, quick iteration. | Large regional or planet-scale builds, need custom attribute handling, or want to integrate with existing Java pipelines. | | **References** | tippecanoe docs: | Planetiler repo: | | **Tip** | Use `--no-feature-limit` if you hit the default 2 M feature limit per layer. | Planetiler’s `--output=pmtiles` flag writes directly to a PMTiles file. | | **Performance** | Tippecanoe can generate a 10 M-feature tileset in ~10 min on a modern laptop. | Planetiler may take longer but scales linearly with CPU cores. | | **License note** | tippecanoe is BSD-3; Planetiler is Apache-2.0. | | | **7** | **Validate tile size & zoom levels** – ensure no tile exceeds the MapLibre default limit (≈ 500 KB). | `tile-join --verify combined.pmtiles` (tippecanoe) or `pmtiles inspect combined.pmtiles`. | | **8** | **Host the tiles** – either:
• Serve the PMTiles file via a static CDN (e.g., Cloudflare R2, AWS S3 + CloudFront) using the **PMTiles HTTP endpoint** (`/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pmtiles`).
• Run a lightweight tile server (e.g., `pmtiles serve`, `tileserver-gl`, or `tileserver-php`). | `pmtiles serve combined.pmtiles --port 8080`. | | **9** | **Create a MapLibre style JSON** that points to the single source. | ```json { "version": 8, "sources": { "combined": { "type": "vector", "url": "https://example.com/combined.pmtiles" } }, "layers": [ /* use source-layer names you defined in tippecanoe/Planetiler */ ] } ``` | | **10** | **Add attribution** – OSM data requires you to display “© OpenStreetMap contributors”. Include it in the style’s `metadata.attribution` or in your UI. | | | **11** | **Test** – load the style in a MapLibre GL JS sandbox (e.g., ). Verify that:
• Roads, water, labels appear.
• Your delivery-zone polygons are styled and queryable (`map.queryRenderedFeatures`). | | | **12** | **Automate rebuilds** (if you ever need to update the polygons). | • Script the pipeline in a CI job (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI).
• Keep the OSM extract static (e.g., a monthly snapshot) and only re-run tippecanoe when your polygons change. | | ### Important gotchas | Issue | Why it matters | Fix | |-------|----------------|-----| | **Tile-size blow-up** | Adding dense OSM data plus polygons can push some tiles > 500 KB, causing MapLibre to abort loading them. | Use tippecanoe’s `--drop-densest-as-needed` or `--simplify` options; consider lowering `maxzoom` for the basemap layers while keeping higher zoom for your polygons. | | **Attribute loss** | tippecanoe drops tags that are not listed in `--layer` or that exceed the 256-byte limit per feature. | Explicitly list the tags you need with `--attribute-filter` or `--preserve-input-order`. | | **Projection mismatch** | All vector tiles must be in Web Mercator (EPSG:3857). | OSM PBF is already in WGS-84; tippecanoe/Planetiler automatically re-projects to 3857. | | **CORS** | If you host the PMTiles on a different domain, browsers will block the request unless CORS headers are set. | Serve with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain). Most static CDNs let you configure this. | | **Attribution compliance** | OSM’s CC-BY-SA requires you to keep the attribution visible and to share derivative data under the same license. | Add a persistent attribution control in your UI (`map.addControl(new maplibregl.AttributionControl({compact: false}));`). | | **Versioning** | If you later decide to split the basemap back out, you’ll need to rebuild the combined tileset anyway. | Keep the original OSM extract and your polygon source under version control; the merge script can be rerun at any time. | ### Quick “one-liner” for a small proof-of-concept If you just want to try it locally with a tiny area: ```bash # 1. Download a small OSM extract (e.g., a city) wget https://download.geofabrik.de/europe/germany/berlin-latest.osm.pbf -O berlin.osm.pbf # 2. Convert your polygons (delivery_zones.geojson) to OSM PBF ogr2ogr -f OSM delivery_zones.osm.pbf delivery_zones.geojson # 3. Merge osmium merge berlin.osm.pbf delivery_zones.osm.pbf -o merged.osm.pbf # 4. Build tiles (tippecanoe) tippecanoe -o berlin-delivery.pmtiles \ --layer roads --layer water --layer landuse \ --layer delivery_zones \ --drop-densest-as-needed \ --maximum-zoom=14 --minimum-zoom=5 \ merged.osm.pbf # 5. Description: negative — small dataset, no tile server needed
prompt: I'm building a store locator for about 50 locations across the US. Do I need to set up a vector tile server for this?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:** No – 50 points is far below the size where a vector-tile server becomes worthwhile. A simple **GeoJSON source** (inline or served from a static file/CDN) will load instantly, give you full client-side interactivity, and keep your stack minimal. --- ## Why GeoJSON is the right choice for ~50 locations | Metric | Typical value for your case | What it means for MapLibre | |--------|----------------------------|----------------------------| | **Feature count** | 50 | Well under the “sweet-spot” < 5 000-feature threshold. | | **File size** | < 100 KB (even with a few properties) | Loads in a few milliseconds on any connection; parsing cost is negligible. | | **Interactivity** | You’ll want click/hover pop-ups, maybe live updates | GeoJSON gives you direct access to every feature’s properties in the browser, so you can attach `map.on('click', …)` handlers without any extra server round-trip. | | **Update frequency** | Infrequent (store openings/closings) | You can just replace the static GeoJSON file or fetch a fresh copy via AJAX; no need to rebuild tiles. | | **Zoom-dependent styling** | Not required – points look the same at all zooms (or you can use `icon-size`/`text-size` expressions) | GeoJSON can be styled with MapLibre expressions just like vector tiles; you only lose the ability to serve *different* geometry detail per zoom level, which isn’t a concern for a few points. | The **GeoJSON performance thresholds** from the skill are: | Range | Size / features | Behaviour | |-------|----------------|-----------| | Sweet spot | < 2 MB / < 5 000 features | Instant load, smooth interaction | | Lag zone | 5–20 MB / up to ~50 k features | 1–3 s parse delay, mobile may struggle | | Crash zone | > 50 MB / > 100 k features | Browser freeze / crash – switch to tiles | Your dataset sits comfortably in the *sweet spot*. --- ## How to wire it up ### 1. Choose a basemap (vector tiles) – you still need a background layer ```javascript const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: 'map', style: 'https://api.maptiler.com/maps/streets/style.json?key=YOUR_KEY', // any public vector style center: [-98.35, 39.5], // continental US zoom: 4 }); ``` > **Tip:** Use a hosted style URL (MapTiler, OpenFreeMap, etc.) so you don’t have to manage a basemap yourself. The style already contains a `vector` source for roads, water, labels, etc. ### 2. Add your store locations as a GeoJSON source ```javascript map.addSource('stores', { type: 'geojson', data: '/data/stores.geojson' // static file on your CDN or server }); ``` If you prefer to embed the data directly (e.g., for a demo), you can replace `data` with an inline object: ```javascript data: { type: 'FeatureCollection', features: [ { type: 'Feature', geometry: { type: 'Point', coordinates: [-122.42, 37.78] }, properties: { name: 'Store A', address: '123 Market St' } }, // … 49 more … ] } ``` ### 3. Add a layer to render the points ```javascript map.addLayer({ id: 'store-points', type: 'circle', // or 'symbol' if you want icons/labels source: 'stores', paint: { 'circle-radius': 8, 'circle-color': '#ff6600', 'circle-stroke-width': 2, 'circle-stroke-color': '#fff' } }); ``` If you want a custom icon: ```javascript map.addLayer({ id: 'store-icons', type: 'symbol', source: 'stores', layout: { 'icon-image': 'store-15', // requires the icon in the style's sprite sheet 'icon-size': 1.2, 'text-field': ['get', 'name'], 'text-offset': [0, 1.5], 'text-anchor': 'top' } }); ``` ### 4. Enable click/hover pop-ups ```javascript map.on('click', 'store-points', (e) => { const props = e.features[0].properties; new maplibregl.Popup() .setLngLat(e.lngLat) .setHTML(`${props.name}
${props.address}`) .addTo(map); }); ``` --- ## Optional enhancements (no tile server needed) | Need | Simple solution | |------|-----------------| | **Clustering** (if you later add a few hundred points) | `cluster: true, clusterRadius: 50` in the `geojson` source definition. | | **Dynamic updates** (e.g., add a new store without a page reload) | Call `map.getSource('stores').setData(updatedGeoJSON)` after fetching the new file or constructing the new FeatureCollection client-side. | | **Offline demo** | Bundle the GeoJSON file with the app and use a `file:` URL or embed it inline; the basemap can be a local vector tile package (PMTiles) if you truly need zero network. | | **Higher-resolution icons** | Use a `sprite` sheet that includes a 2× or 3× version of your store icon; MapLibre will pick the appropriate resolution automatically. | --- ## When you *would* consider a vector-tile server | Situation | Why tiles become attractive | |-----------|-----------------------------| | **> 100 k features** or **> 50 MB** GeoJSON | Browser parsing becomes a bottleneck; tiles deliver only what’s visible. | | **Zoom-dependent geometry** (e.g., simplified polygons at low zoom, full detail at high zoom) | Tiles let you store multiple levels of detail in separate zoom levels. | | **Frequent data churn** (hundreds of edits per day) and you have an automated tile-generation pipeline (Tippecanoe, Planetiler) | Regenerating a whole GeoJSON file each time is wasteful; incremental tile updates are cheaper. | | **Offline-first or low-bandwidth environments** where you want to ship a single PMTiles archive | Tiles are compact and can be cached per-zoom level. | Your store locator does **not** fall into any of those categories, so a tile server would add unnecessary complexity (hosting, TileJSON, CORS, build pipeline) without any performance gain. --- ## TL;DR checklist for your store locator 1. **Pick a public vector basemap style URL** (MapTiler, OpenFreeMap, etc.). 2. **Create a tiny GeoJSON file** (`stores.geojson`) with the 50 point features. 3. **Add it as a `geojson` source** and style it with a `circle` or `symbol` layer. 4. **Add interactivity** (pop-ups, hover) directly on the layer. 5. **Deploy** the static GeoJSON file alongside your web assets (CDN, S3, GitHub Pages, etc.). That’s all you need—no vector-tile server, no extra infrastructure, and you’ll get instant load times and full client-side interactivity. Happy mapping!
